# `perfectionist::numeric_escape_for_visible_character`

- _Default state:_ `active`
- _Source:_ [`src/rules/numeric_escape_for_visible_character.rs`](../src/rules/numeric_escape_for_visible_character.rs)

> visible character written as a numeric escape; spell the character as itself

## What it does

Forbids a visible character written as a numeric escape in a
string, character, or C-string literal, and suggests the
character itself in its place. The escapes it reads are
`\xNN` and `\u{...}`.

A character counts as visible when it occupies at least one
terminal column, is not whitespace, and is not a Private Use
Area codepoint; the `flag_non_ascii` knob narrows that set to
the ASCII characters. So `\u{2192}` is flagged, while `\u{0}` (a
control character), `\u{9}` (a tab), `\u{A0}` (a no-break
space), `\u{200B}` (zero width), `\u{301}` (a combining mark)
and `\u{E0B0}` (private use) are not. Each of those either has
no glyph of its own or has none a reader could pick out from
its neighbours, which is where the escape is the clearer
spelling.

An escape stays as it is where the literal cannot hold its
character verbatim: the closing delimiter (`\x22` in a string
or C-string literal, `\x27` in a character literal) and the
backslash (`\x5C`). Byte literals (`b"..."`, `b'...'`) are out
of scope, because a `\xNN` there denotes one byte rather than
one character and above `\x7F` no character spells that byte;
`\xNN` above `\x7F` in a C-string literal is left alone for
the same reason.

Every string, character, and C-string literal in the crate's
own source is scanned, including one inside a macro invocation
and one a `#[cfg(...)]` excludes from the build. A file
reached through `include_str!` or `include_bytes!` is data
rather than Rust, so it is skipped.

The rewrite preserves the literal's value, the decoded
character being the same either way. A `format!`-family
template keeps its meaning too: the placeholder grammar
applies to the decoded text, so `\u{7B}` already opens a
placeholder before the rewrite spells it `{`.

## Why restrict this?

This is a stylistic preference, not a correctness issue. An
escape hides what the literal says: a reader has to decode
`\u{2192}` to learn that the string holds an arrow, a reviewer
cannot tell the arrow from any other codepoint at a glance,
and a search for the character itself finds nothing. Spelling
the character makes the literal read as the text it is, and
keeps one spelling for a character wherever it appears. Source
files are UTF-8, so the escape buys no portability in
exchange.

## Interaction with sibling rules

Spelling the character out can hand it to a rule that forbids
the character itself, and the two then compose into a two-step
fix rather than fighting: a `\u{2026}` in a panic message is
spelled out by this rule, which
`perfectionist::unicode_ellipsis_in_panic_messages` then
reports, so the pair lands on the ASCII three-dot form it
wants.

## Interaction with Clippy

`clippy::invisible_characters` (`correctness`, deny by
default) is this rule's mirror image. Where a character has no
glyph of its own, such as a zero-width space or a soft hyphen,
it reports the character and asks for the escape; this rule
reports the escape and asks for the character. An invisible
character is one this rule declines by definition, so the two
never ask opposite things about the same character, and
together they read as one policy: escape what has no glyph,
spell out what has one.

`clippy::unicode_not_nfc` (`pedantic`, off by default) reports
a decomposed sequence and asks for the precomposed form. It
reads the literal as written, so an escape anywhere in the
sequence hides it: `"caf\u{65}"` followed by a combining acute
goes unreported until the escape is spelled out, at which
point Clippy sees `"cafe"` plus the mark and composes it. This
rule never flags a combining mark, so it only ever hands that
lint work it could not otherwise reach.

`clippy::non_ascii_literal` (`restriction`, off by default) is
the one that disagrees. It forbids a non-ASCII character
written as itself and asks for the escape, which is the
opposite request on the same literal. Running both is a matter
of setting `flag_non_ascii = false`, which leaves this rule
the ASCII half the two agree on, such as `\x41` for `A`, and
leaves the non-ASCII escapes to Clippy.

## Example

**Avoid:**

```rust,ignore
let arrow = "\u{2192}";
let name = "Ren\u{E9}";
let letter = '\x41';
```

**Prefer:**

```rust,ignore
let arrow = "→";
let name = "René";
let letter = 'A';
```

## Configuration

Configure via `dylint.toml` under `["perfectionist::numeric_escape_for_visible_character"]`. Every field is optional; the per-field prose below states the default.

### Field: `flag_non_ascii`

- _Type:_ `boolean`
- _Optional_

Flag an escape whose character is outside ASCII, such as
`\u{2192}` for `→`. Defaults to `true`. Set it to `false` to
keep only the ASCII half of the rule, such as `\x41` for `A`.
